text: Horizons was a suspended omnimover dark ride located in the eastern section of Future World (now World Discovery) at Epcot, which was then known as EPCOT Center, a theme park in Bay Lake, Florida. The attraction depicted possible life in the 21st century across land, under the sea, and in outer space, and is believed to be the sequel to Walt Disney's Carousel of Progress, which is located in Tomorrowland at Magic Kingdom. Horizons was the only attraction in Future World to showcase all of EPCOT's "Future World" themes: communication, energy, transportation, anatomy, and humanity’s relationship with land and sea. It officially opened on October 1, 1983, as part of Phase II of Epcot. The ride originally closed on December 25, 1994, just over a year after General Electric ended its sponsorship, which expired on September 30, 1993. Following the sponsorship end, all references to GE were removed, and the attraction began experiencing technical issues due to deteriorating animatronics and frequent breakdowns. Horizons re-opened on December 24, 1995, due to the closures of Universe of Energy and World of Motion for refurbishment, and operated until its permanent closure on January 9, 1999. After closing, the building was dismantled and demolished to make way for Mission: Space, which opened on October 9, 2003. The original concept name was Century 3 (or Century III), representing the third century of American existence (1976–2076), but it was changed to Futureprobe to appeal to international guests, though that name was later abandoned due to its medical connotation. The final name chosen was Horizons. Before construction began, the project’s budget was reduced by $10 million, the building size was reduced, and the ride length was shortened by 35%, or 600 feet (180 m). Horizons opened exactly one year after Epcot’s opening and was situated between World of Motion and the Universe of Energy. In 1989, the Wonders of Life pavilion became its neighbor, and World of Motion closed in 1996, with Horizons remaining open until Test Track opened in early 1999. The ride’s concept originated with Reginald Jones and Jack Welch of General Electric, initially focusing on Thomas Edison and GE’s history, but shifted to focus on the future of America, later adjusted to appeal to a global audience. The building was designed to resemble a spaceship, emphasizing three-dimensionality and the idea of an infinite horizon. The ride began with a section titled "Looking Back at Tomorrow," showing visions from Jules Verne and Albert Robida through the 1950s, followed by two OMNIMAX screens displaying futuristic technologies. The main portion, "Tomorrow's Windows," featured a family living in Nova Cite, with the daughter managing irrigation robots at Mesa Verde, communicating via video chat with her marine biologist boyfriend at Sea Castle, and celebrating a birthday at the space station Brava Centauri through holographic teleconferencing. Horizons was the only Disney attraction with multiple endings, allowing guests to choose one of three paths—Brava Centauri, Mesa Verde, or Sea Castle—by pressing a button, resulting in a 31-second video sequence showing a simulated flyover of a futuristic landscape. These videos were created using scale models, some of the largest ever built at the time, such as the 32 by 75 feet (9.8 by 22.9 m) desert model, filmed in a hangar at Burbank Airport over a year by 30 model makers. The exit corridor originally featured Robert T. McCall’s mural, "The Prologue and the Promise," which was removed before demolition and is now unknown. Some Horizons props were displayed at various locations, including EPCOT: Creating the World of Tomorrow, Disney’s Hollywood Studios warehouse, and Walt Disney Studios Park’s Backlot Tour, though many have since been removed. The McCall mural, the robot butler, and other artifacts are now in private collections. Some of the attraction’s robots appeared in the entry mural of Innoventions. Tributes to Horizons remain in Mission: SPACE, including the attraction logo on the gravity wheel’s center and a stylized version on the Cargo Bay gift shop checkout counter, and a new mural added in 2017 featuring Brava Centauri. The concrete planter west of the current attraction reflects the original building’s shape and where the main sign once stood. Space Mountain includes tributes, and in the post-show, props from Horizons were once displayed in the exhibition gallery at Disney’s Hollywood Studios. In the queue of Guardians of the Galaxy: Cosmic Rewind at Tokyo Disneyland, Peter Quill mentions visiting EPCOT Center as a child and wanting to ride Horizons again, unaware it had closed since 1987. At the exit of Star Tours - The Adventures Continue in Tokyo Disneyland, a kiosk plays the full 31-second endings from Horizons—Mesa Verde, Brava Centauri, and Sea Castle (set on planet Praya)—in their unedited form.
